lesson.menu_desc: One deal, three countries: cross-border, counterpart, local counsel, exchange rate, withholding tax, double taxation, antitrust clearance, condition precedent, apostille, prevailing language -- and comparatives and superlatives to compare jurisdictions -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 25 -- Cross-Border Transactions -- One Deal, Three Countries
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 25 -- Cross-Border Transactions
lesson.grammar_point: comparatives and superlatives to compare jurisdictions (-er than / more ... than / less ... than / as ... as / the most)

listenings.text: Simone, it is Javier, from the legal team in Madrid. Before tomorrow's call with New York, here is where the Campinas deal stands, country by country. This is a cross-border deal, so we have three sets of rules on one table. The seller is a fund in New York, the buyer is our group here in Madrid, and the target is in Brazil. The Brazilian side is the most complicated part. We need antitrust clearance from CADE before we can close, and CADE is slower than the authority in Spain. Our local counsel in Sao Paulo says it usually takes about ninety days, so that clearance is a condition precedent in the contract. The Spanish side is easier than the Brazilian side, but it is not as fast as I would like. Every power of attorney we sign here needs an apostille before it is valid in Brazil. And then there is the money. The price is in dollars, and the exchange rate moved again this week, so the real cost in euros is higher than last month. One more thing for you. Ask their counsel about withholding tax on the payment. We do not want double taxation, with two countries taxing the same money.

Hi Simone, this is Rachel Moore, counsel for the seller in New York. I am sorry to leave this on your voicemail, but the time difference makes it hard to find a slot. Three quick points before our call. First, the contract. We have an English version and a Portuguese version, and we want English as the prevailing language. For us, one language is safer than two languages with the same weight. Second, the closing date. I understand that the clearance in Brazil is the longest step in the whole deal, so we can accept a later date, but not later than the end of March. Third, tax. Our fund is based in the United States, and our tax advisors say the Brazilian withholding tax is higher than the rate we expected. Can your local counsel check whether the tax treaty makes it lower? Your counterpart on the tax side is Tom Walsh, and he is the best person to talk to. Talk tomorrow at nine New York time, which I think is ten in Sao Paulo.

extra_audio.text: First, you map the deal: which countries are involved, who your counterpart is on each side, and which law governs the contract. Then, you hire local counsel in each country, because the rules there are different from the rules at home. After that, you list every condition precedent, and you start the slowest one first, which is usually the antitrust clearance. Next, you check the money: the exchange rate, the withholding tax, and whether a treaty prevents double taxation. Finally, you agree on the prevailing language and get an apostille on every document that has to travel.
